title: The head, the pillar, the peak
hookLine: Mu'adh asks what leads to the garden, and is told of worship, the doors of good, and to guard his tongue
tomorrow: some things Allah left unsaid, on purpose. how is that mercy?

cards: The reply is already typed. Three lines, every word true, sharp enough to end something. A thumb hovers over send.
Now a road in Arabia, long ago.

A young man named Mu'adh ibn Jabal is traveling with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and one morning he comes up close and asks a huge question: tell me a deed that brings me into the garden and keeps me from the Fire.
The Prophet says: you've asked about something great, and it's easy for the one Allah makes it easy for. Then he starts to build.

teach.h: THE GROUND FLOOR AND THE DOORS.
teach.b: First the ground floor: worship Allah and join nothing to Him, pray, give zakah, fast Ramadan, make the pilgrimage.
Then the doors of good: fasting is a shield, charity puts out a sin the way water puts out fire, and prayer in the middle of the night.
Then a picture, in paraphrase from Tirmidhi's collection: shall I tell you the head of the whole matter, its pillar, and its peak? The head is Islam. The pillar is prayer.
The peak is jihad, striving in Allah's path. A whole building, top to bottom. And here's the twist.
He asks: shall I tell you what holds all of that together?

teach.h: HE TAKES HOLD OF HIS TONGUE.
teach.b: And he takes hold of his own tongue and says: restrain this. Mu'adh is honestly surprised. Will we really be held to account for what we say?
The answer comes back as a question: what throws people on their faces into the Fire, if not the harvest of their tongues?
That's the detail to tell a friend tonight. After the head, the pillar and the peak, the Prophet points at something small enough to fit behind the teeth.
And a harvest is what you planted, one careless word at a time, without noticing each one was a seed.

how: Muslims who study al-Nawawi's forty learn this hadith as a summary of the faith: the pillars first, then voluntary fasting, charity and night prayer, with guarding the tongue as what keeps it all safe.

o: the top of a building of faith: Islam itself
the first chapter of a book of hadith
a leader who runs the local mosque each week

s: guarding the tongue means never speaking up
the hadith is about the harvest of careless words, not about staying silent when speech is needed.
the Prophet took hold of his own tongue to make the point
he held it and said: restrain this.
Mu'adh already expected words to count as much as deeds
he was surprised: will we really be held to account for what we say?

games.q: you had a solid week: on time, helpful at home, kind at school. on the ride home you tear into a cousin, in detail. what does Mu'adh's hadith say about the week?
o: a good week outweighs one rant; deeds count more than words.
the words are part of the harvest too; the tongue can tip the building.
it doesn't count if everything you said was true.
games.why: after the head, the pillar and the peak, the Prophet held his tongue: restrain this. what throws people on their faces is the harvest of their tongues.

practice: Rest the tip of your tongue lightly behind your top teeth and let your jaw go soft. For the sit, each time a sentence starts to form, notice it arrive, and let it stay unsaid for now.
Nothing is being silenced forever; you're just watching the seeds before they're planted.

wordCard.voice: The head. In the Prophet's picture, the head of the matter is Islam, the pillar is prayer, the peak is striving. And the tongue holds all of it.

orig.note: Arabic: the head of the matter is Islam. the first part of the Prophet's picture for Mu'adh.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: guard the tongue, the small key to a big building. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2616 (Mu'adh ibn Jabal: the head of the matter, its pillar and its peak; the harvest of the tongues)
